title: Critical Readings: Feminism, Marxism and Tragedy
welcome_lead: Engage with the major critical lenses on Tess — feminist, Marxist, and tragic — that examiners reward at AO5.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on critical readings of Hardy's Tess: feminist, Marxist, and classical tragedy approaches.
final_note: AO5 rewards the student who can hold multiple critical lenses in productive tension, not the one who picks a winner.

walkthroughs.body_html: Penny Boumelha's Thomas Hardy and Women (1982) argues that Hardy's narrator is implicated in the very objectification the novel appears to critique. Descriptions of Tess's mouth ('mobile peony mouth') sexualise her in the act of defending her purity. A nuanced response acknowledges this contradiction rather than treating Hardy as straightforwardly feminist or misogynist.

Raymond Williams in The Country and the City (1973) locates Tess's tragedy in the historical breakdown of the rural community: enclosure, migration, and proletarianisation. Tess is not a victim of fate but of capital. The Durbeyfields' eviction after John's death dramatises the loss of 'lifeholds' that historically uprooted late-Victorian peasantry.

Hardy explicitly invokes Aeschylus at the close. Critics debate whether Tess is an Aristotelian tragedy (hamartia, peripeteia, catharsis), a Shakespearean tragedy of character, or a distinctly modern tragedy in Raymond Williams's sense — where ordinary life itself becomes the tragic field. The novel's hybridity is itself an AO3/AO5 talking point.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator's views are always the author's views.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
